practices.name: Behavioral Signals & Analytics
practices.meta_description: Behavioral analytics consulting that finds the signals in noisy, siloed data and turns them into predictive KPIs, testable hypotheses and sound experiments.
practices.tagline: Find the behaviors that predict your outcomes, then measure and test what actually moves them.
intro: Every outcome an organization cares about, from conversion and adoption to retention, adherence and engagement, is the sum of human behaviors. Those behaviors leave traces in transaction logs, CRM records, product telemetry, call notes, surveys and scheduling systems. Most organizations collect this data in abundance, yet still steer by lagging indicators and quarterly surprises. Our behavioral signals and analytics practice exists to close that gap: to read the behavior already recorded in your systems and turn it into measures that tell you what is about to happen.

The work rests on Behavioral Signals Design, our proprietary method for building more predictive KPIs. We start from the outcome that matters, map the journey and the data around it, and identify the few behavioral moments and behavioral types that actually drive results. Along the way we surface the untested assumptions quietly filling gaps in the data, convert them into hypotheses, and design the experiments and pilots that confirm or retire them. The result is a smaller set of measures that leaders can trust and act on.

Our analysts combine research methods, psychometrics and behavioral science with practical data engineering. We integrate data across systems that were never designed to talk to each other, apply cohort and survival analysis where timing matters, build surveys that measure what they claim to measure, and design dashboards for decisions rather than decoration. Every engagement follows our Observe, Signal, Design, Test, Scale method, so analysis always connects to action and to a measurable test.

themes.title: Predictive, not just descriptive
themes.body: Dashboards that report last quarter are useful for accountability, but they rarely help anyone change the next quarter. We focus on leading indicators: the early behaviors that reliably precede conversion, churn, adoption or disengagement. When a measure predicts an outcome and is something a team can influence, it becomes a KPI worth managing. When it does neither, we recommend retiring it.

themes.title: Behavior over demographics
themes.body: Age, region and job title describe who someone is. They say far less about what that person will do next. We define segments and typologies by observed behavior, such as how people explore, hesitate, commit or drift away, because behavioral types point directly to the design changes, messages and service moments that can shift their trajectory.

themes.title: Evidence you can act on
themes.body: Analysis is only finished when it produces a decision or a test. Each finding we deliver is paired with a hypothesis, a proposed intervention and an experiment design, including sample size, primary metric and guardrails. Leaders get clarity about what is known, what is assumed and what is worth testing next, instead of another report that sits unread.

practices.name: Behavioral Design & Experience
practices.meta_description: Behavioral design, experience research and service design that make the right action easier for customers, users, patients and staff, tested before it scales.
practices.tagline: Design products, services and journeys that make the right behavior the easy behavior.
intro: People rarely fail to act because they lack information. They stall because a step is confusing, a moment is mistimed, a choice feels risky or the effort outweighs the perceived reward. Our behavioral design and experience practice applies behavioral science, human-computer interaction and service design to remove those barriers. We help organizations design the products, journeys, communications and service moments that make it easier for people to do what they already want to do, whether that means buying, enrolling, adopting, adhering or returning.

The practice draws on clinical and health psychology, persuasive technology and human-computer interaction. We draw on the Fogg Behavior Model, which holds that behavior occurs when motivation, ability and a prompt converge, along with usability principles, self-determination theory and behavioral economics. Theory guides the questions we ask. Careful research with real people, in real contexts, shapes the answers.

Design work at our firm is always paired with measurement. We begin by observing how people actually behave, use behavioral signals to locate the moments that matter, design targeted changes, and test them through usability studies, pilots and A/B tests before recommending broad rollout. We also hold a clear ethical line: persuasive design should be transparent and aligned with the person's own goals, never manipulative. That standard protects your customers, and it protects your reputation.

themes.title: Research with real people
themes.body: Interviews, contextual inquiry, think-aloud usability sessions and diary studies reveal what analytics alone cannot: the hesitation before a click, the workaround a staff member invented, the moment a patient decides a program is not for them. We pair this qualitative depth with behavioral data so that design decisions rest on both what people do and why.

themes.title: Design for motivation, ability and prompts
themes.body: When a desired behavior is not happening, one of three things is usually missing: enough motivation, enough ability, or a well-timed prompt. Diagnosing which one is absent prevents expensive misfires, such as running a motivational campaign when the real problem is a confusing form. Our designs target the specific barrier, which keeps changes small, focused and testable.

themes.title: Ethical persuasion by default
themes.body: Persuasive technology can help people build healthy habits, complete important tasks and adopt useful tools. It can also exploit attention and erode trust. We design for transparency, informed choice and easy exit, and we review every intervention against the person's own interests. Behavior change that people would endorse on reflection is the only kind that lasts.

services.name: Behavioral Signals Design
services.meta_title: Behavioral Signals Design: Predictive KPI Method
services.meta_description: Behavioral Signals Design is our method for finding the conversion points and behavioral types in your data and turning them into predictive KPIs and A/B tests.
services.summary: Our signature method for finding the behaviors that predict your outcomes and turning them into predictive KPIs, testable hypotheses and focused experiments.
services.lede: Behavioral Signals Design is our proprietary method for building more predictive KPIs. It locates the conversion points and behavioral types hidden in noisy, siloed data, exposes untested assumptions, and turns them into hypotheses and experiments.
challenge: Most organizations measure what is easy to count rather than what predicts the outcome they care about. Revenue, enrollments, churn and satisfaction scores arrive after the fact, when the behavior that produced them is already finished. Meanwhile the early signals sit scattered across a CRM, a product database, a call center platform, a scheduling tool and a survey vendor, each owned by a different team and keyed to a different identifier. No one can see the whole journey, so no one can see which moments in it actually matter.

Into those gaps flow assumptions. A sales team believes a demo drives purchase. A product team believes a feature drives retention. A clinical team believes reminders drive adherence. Some of these beliefs are correct, and some are expensive guesses that have never been tested. Because the assumptions are invisible, they shape budgets, staffing and roadmaps without scrutiny. Behavioral signals design exists to make those assumptions visible, test them against the data, and replace the ones that fail with measures that genuinely predict performance.

approach.title: Anchor on the outcome and the journey
approach.body: We start by agreeing on the single outcome that matters most, such as conversion, adoption, retention or adherence, and defining it precisely enough to measure. Through stakeholder interviews, contextual inquiry and journey mapping we document every step people take toward or away from that outcome, plus every system that records those steps. We also capture the working beliefs each team holds about what drives results.

approach.title: Find conversion points and behavioral types
approach.body: We integrate data across siloed systems, resolve identities, and build an event-level view of the journey. Using cohort analysis, survival analysis and sequence modeling, we identify the few conversion points where trajectories diverge and the behavioral types that move through them differently. Each candidate signal is tested for lead time, stability across cohorts and whether a team can actually influence it.

approach.title: Turn assumptions into hypotheses and KPIs
approach.body: We place each untested assumption beside the evidence and rewrite it as a falsifiable hypothesis. Signals that survive become predictive KPIs with clear definitions, owners, thresholds and refresh rates. For each KPI we use the Fogg Behavior Model to diagnose whether motivation, ability or a missing prompt is the constraint, then specify the intervention most likely to move it.

approach.title: Run focused A/B tests and pilots
approach.body: Every hypothesis gets an experiment plan before anything is built: the primary metric, a minimum detectable effect, a power calculation, guardrail metrics to catch harm, and stopping rules. Where randomization is impractical we design staged pilots or matched comparisons. Results confirm which KPIs truly lead the outcome and which interventions move them, and which assumptions should be retired.

approach.title: Embed the signals in decisions
approach.body: Validated KPIs move into operating rhythms: decision dashboards, weekly reviews, alert thresholds and team goals. We document the data pipeline so it survives staff changes, coach leaders on interpreting leading indicators without overreacting to noise, and set a cadence for retesting as markets and behavior shift. The method becomes a capability your teams can run themselves.

deliverables: Integrated journey and data map across source systems
Conversion point analysis with cohort and survival curves
Behavioral typology with sizing and trajectory profiles
Assumption register converted into testable hypotheses
Predictive KPI definitions with owners and thresholds
Powered experiment plans with guardrail metrics
outcomes: Leaders see early warning of performance changes instead of learning about them after the quarter closes.
Teams focus effort on the few behavioral moments that measurably drive the outcome.
Untested assumptions are replaced by evidence, reducing spending on initiatives that were never going to work.
Experiments are designed to produce clear answers, so each test builds organizational knowledge.
services.who_we_serve: Behavioral signals design serves chief executives, chief growth and marketing officers, product leaders, heads of analytics and operations, and health system and association executives. It suits organizations with plenty of data but little confidence in which numbers to manage, often after a merger, a platform migration, a stalled growth plan or a board request for better forward-looking metrics. Private equity sponsors also use it to establish predictive KPIs in a new portfolio company.
services.impact_lens: Predictive KPIs built on real behavior benefit more than the income statement. Customers and users encounter fewer dead ends because friction is found and fixed early. Patients and members receive support at the moment it helps rather than after they disengage. Employees are measured on behaviors they can influence, which is fairer and more motivating. And because the method replaces guesses with evidence, scarce resources in health, education and community programs go further toward the people they are meant to serve.

faqs.q: How is behavioral signals design different from a standard analytics engagement?
faqs.a: A standard analytics engagement usually starts with the data and describes it. Behavioral signals design starts with the outcome and the human behaviors that produce it, then looks for the specific moments and behavioral types that predict it. It also treats untested assumptions as first-class objects to be tested. The end product is not a report but a short list of predictive KPIs, each linked to a hypothesis and an experiment.

faqs.q: What if our data is spread across systems that have never been integrated?
faqs.a: That is the normal starting point. We map each source, define the identifiers and timestamps that can link them, and build an integrated event-level view of the journey, often in a lightweight analytical environment before any permanent infrastructure is changed. Where linkage is imperfect, we quantify the gaps and design around them, and we recommend the minimum data changes needed to keep the signals reliable.

faqs.q: How do you know a signal is truly predictive and not just correlated?
faqs.a: We look for lead time, consistency across cohorts and time periods, and a plausible behavioral mechanism. Survival and cohort analysis show whether the signal precedes the outcome. Holdout periods check whether it predicts out of sample. Ultimately, the strongest evidence comes from experiments: if changing the behavior changes the outcome, the signal is a genuine lever rather than a coincidence.

faqs.q: How long does a behavioral signals design engagement take?
faqs.a: Timing depends on the number of systems involved, data access and the complexity of the journey. A focused engagement on one outcome and one journey typically moves from discovery to an initial set of predictive KPIs and experiment plans in a matter of weeks to a few months. Testing and scaling then run on the cadence your traffic, enrollment or sales cycle allows.

services.name: Predictive KPI Design
services.meta_title: Predictive KPI Design: Leading Indicators That Work
services.meta_description: Predictive KPI design that replaces lagging and vanity metrics with behavior-based leading indicators your teams can influence, validate and manage weekly.
services.summary: Replace lagging and vanity metrics with behavior-based leading indicators that forecast results and give teams something they can actually influence.
services.lede: Predictive KPIs tell you what is likely to happen while there is still time to change it. We design behavior-based leading indicators that are validated against your outcomes, owned by the right teams and built into everyday decisions.
challenge: Most KPI sets grow by accumulation. Each initiative adds a metric, few are ever removed, and the scorecard becomes a long list of lagging results and activity counts. Revenue, net promoter scores and churn rates tell leaders how the last period went, but not what to do this week. Activity metrics such as calls made or emails sent are easy to inflate and loosely connected to results. Teams learn to hit the number rather than move the outcome.

Predictive KPIs fix this by measuring the behaviors that reliably precede an outcome and that a team can influence. Finding them takes more than intuition. A candidate indicator has to show lead time, hold up across segments and periods, resist gaming and come with a clear owner. Without that rigor, organizations simply swap one set of vanity metrics for another, add complexity without insight, and lose credibility with the people asked to manage them.

approach.title: Audit the current scorecard
approach.body: We inventory existing KPIs, trace how each is calculated, and interview the people who report and use them. For every metric we ask what decision it informs, how quickly it responds, and whether anyone can influence it. This reveals redundant, lagging and easily gamed measures and clarifies which outcomes leaders actually need to forecast.

approach.title: Identify candidate leading indicators
approach.body: Using historical data, we test candidate behaviors for their relationship to the target outcome, examining lead time, effect size and stability across cohorts. Survival analysis shows how early a signal appears before churn or conversion. We favor indicators rooted in specific customer, user or employee behaviors over composite scores that hide what is actually changing.

approach.title: Define KPIs with owners and thresholds
approach.body: Each selected KPI receives a precise operational definition, data source, refresh frequency, accountable owner and action threshold. We pair leading and lagging measures so teams can see cause and consequence together, and we document known ways each metric could be gamed along with the counter-metric that guards against it.

approach.title: Validate predictive power in practice
approach.body: We back-test KPIs against held-out periods and then run them forward in parallel with the existing scorecard. Where possible we run a targeted experiment that moves the leading behavior to confirm that the lagging outcome follows. Indicators that fail to predict, or that cannot be moved, are revised or dropped.

approach.title: Build KPIs into operating rhythm
approach.body: Validated predictive KPIs are integrated into dashboards, planning cycles, incentive discussions and weekly reviews. We train managers to read leading indicators as probabilities rather than verdicts, set review cadences that avoid overreaction to noise, and establish a governance process for adding, retiring and recalibrating metrics over time.

deliverables: Current KPI audit with retire, keep and revise recommendations
Leading indicator analysis with lead time and stability tests
KPI dictionary with definitions, sources and owners
Paired leading and lagging measure framework
Back-test and forward validation report
KPI governance and recalibration playbook
outcomes: Leadership conversations shift from explaining past results to acting on early signals.
Teams manage a shorter list of measures that they can genuinely influence.
Metric gaming declines because every KPI has a defined counter-metric and owner.
Forecasts become more reliable because they rest on validated behavioral precursors.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief operating and financial officers, heads of strategy and analytics, sales and customer success leaders, and boards seeking better forward visibility. Typical trigger moments include a new strategic plan, a leadership transition, a missed forecast, a shift to a subscription or membership model, or an investor request for leading indicators. Health systems, associations and portfolio companies often engage us when existing scorecards no longer explain performance.
services.impact_lens: Predictive KPIs change who gets helped and when. A member who is drifting away can be reached before they cancel. A patient showing early signs of disengagement can receive support before a missed treatment. Employees benefit from being measured on behaviors they control instead of outcomes shaped by forces beyond them. And in mission-driven organizations, better forward measures mean resources reach communities while intervention can still make a difference.

faqs.q: What makes a KPI predictive rather than lagging?
faqs.a: A predictive KPI measures a behavior or condition that reliably appears before the outcome you care about, with enough lead time to act. A lagging KPI records the outcome itself after it has happened. Revenue is lagging. The share of new customers who complete a key setup step within their first week may be predictive of revenue, if the data shows it consistently precedes renewal or expansion.

faqs.q: How many KPIs should an organization track?
faqs.a: Fewer than most do. We generally recommend a small set of predictive KPIs per outcome, each paired with the lagging result it forecasts and a guardrail that protects against gaming. Additional diagnostic metrics can sit beneath them for analysts, but the measures leaders manage week to week should be few enough that everyone knows what each one means and who owns it.

faqs.q: Can predictive KPIs work if our historical data is limited?
faqs.a: Yes, though the approach adapts. With limited history we rely more heavily on qualitative research and established behavioral science to propose candidate indicators, then validate them prospectively by tracking them forward and running small experiments. Over time the evidence accumulates and the KPI set is refined. Starting with well-reasoned hypotheses is far better than waiting for perfect data.

faqs.q: How do predictive KPIs relate to Behavioral Signals Design?
faqs.a: Behavioral Signals Design is our broader method for finding the conversion points, behavioral types and untested assumptions in a journey. Predictive KPI design is the discipline of turning those findings into well-defined, validated, governed measures. Many clients start with Behavioral Signals Design and then use this service to formalize and maintain their KPI system as it matures.

services.name: Behavioral Data Analysis
services.meta_description: Behavioral data analysis that integrates siloed, noisy datasets and finds the patterns of action that explain conversion, retention, adoption and engagement.
services.summary: Integrate siloed, noisy datasets and find the patterns of human action that explain conversion, retention, adoption and engagement in your organization.
services.lede: Behavioral data analysis examines what people actually do, not just who they are or what they say. We integrate records across your systems, clean the noise and reveal the action patterns that explain your most important outcomes.
challenge: Organizations rarely lack data. They lack data that can be read as behavior. Web analytics captures clicks but not phone calls. The CRM records opportunities but not product usage. The electronic health record captures visits but not what happened between them. Each system uses its own identifiers, definitions and time stamps, and many contain duplicates, gaps and fields that changed meaning after a software upgrade. Analysts spend most of their time reconciling sources and too little time understanding people.

Even when data is assembled, conventional reporting tends to summarize it into averages and totals that erase the sequence and timing of behavior. Yet sequence and timing are usually where the insight lives: who acted first, how long they waited, what they did just before they stopped. Behavioral data analysis restores that view, so leaders can see the decisions and habits underneath the numbers and ask better questions about why they occur.

approach.title: Understand the behavior behind the data
approach.body: Before writing a query we talk with the people who generate and use the data: frontline staff, customers, product managers and analysts. We learn how records are actually created, where workarounds distort them, and which behaviors matter most. This context prevents misreading artifacts of process as signals of behavior and sharpens the analytic questions.

approach.title: Integrate, clean and model events
approach.body: We link sources through shared identifiers or probabilistic matching, standardize definitions, and reshape records into event sequences for each person or account. Then we apply sequence analysis, cohort comparisons, survival models and clustering to find recurring patterns, critical transitions and early divergence between people who succeed and those who stall.

approach.title: Translate patterns into hypotheses
approach.body: Each meaningful pattern is translated into a plain-language behavioral explanation and a testable hypothesis about what would change it. We distinguish clearly between findings with strong evidence and those that are suggestive, and we recommend the specific interventions, messages or process changes most worth testing first.

approach.title: Check findings against new evidence
approach.body: We validate patterns on held-out data and later time periods, and where possible confirm them through small experiments or natural experiments created by policy or product changes. This step prevents organizations from acting on patterns that were artifacts of a single season, campaign or data quirk.

approach.title: Make the analysis repeatable
approach.body: We package the integration logic, behavioral definitions and models into documented, maintainable code and hand them to your team. Recurring analyses become scheduled reports or dashboard views, and we train analysts in the behavioral framing so they can extend the work to new questions without starting over.

deliverables: Data source inventory with linkage and quality assessment
Integrated event-level behavioral dataset
Sequence, cohort and survival analysis findings
Behavioral pattern library in plain language
Prioritized hypothesis list with recommended tests
Documented, reusable analysis code and definitions
outcomes: Leaders understand the behaviors driving results rather than only the results themselves.
Analysts spend less time reconciling sources and more time answering strategic questions.
Interventions target the specific moments where people stall, disengage or drop out.
Data from previously separate systems becomes a coherent view of the customer or member journey.
services.who_we_serve: Our behavioral data analysis supports heads of analytics and data science, product and growth leaders, marketing executives, operations directors and health system quality leaders. It is often requested after a system migration, an acquisition that combined customer bases, a sudden change in retention or conversion, or when an in-house data team has the tools but needs behavioral science expertise to frame the right questions and interpret what they find.
services.impact_lens: Reading data as behavior makes organizations more humane in how they respond. Customers who struggle are seen as people encountering obstacles rather than as churn statistics. Patients who miss appointments can be understood in context and supported accordingly. Employees gain clearer insight into which of their actions matter. We apply strict privacy and minimization practices, analyze only what is needed, and favor uses of data that serve the people who generated it.

faqs.q: What kinds of data do you analyze?
faqs.a: Almost any record of human action: transactions, product and web events, CRM activity, call center logs, appointment and scheduling data, learning management records, survey responses and operational timestamps. We also integrate qualitative data such as interview notes or open-text feedback when it helps explain the patterns. The common thread is that each record reflects a decision or action someone took.

faqs.q: Do you need direct access to our systems?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many engagements work from secure extracts provided by your team, analyzed in an environment that meets your security and privacy requirements. We sign appropriate data agreements, follow the principle of minimum necessary data, and can work with de-identified or pseudonymized records. For health data we align with applicable privacy regulations and your compliance team's protocols.

faqs.q: How is this different from what our BI team already does?
faqs.a: Business intelligence teams typically build reliable reporting on agreed metrics. Behavioral data analysis asks different questions: in what order do people act, where do trajectories split, and what distinguishes those who succeed? It relies on methods such as sequence and survival analysis and on behavioral science to interpret results. We usually work alongside BI teams and hand over methods they can continue to use.

faqs.q: What if our data quality is poor?
faqs.a: Imperfect data is the norm. We assess quality early, quantify missingness and inconsistency, and determine which questions the data can and cannot answer reliably. Often the most useful early finding is a short list of fixes that would dramatically improve data usefulness. Where gaps remain, we triangulate with qualitative research and design prospective measurement to fill them.

services.name: Conversion Behavior Analytics
services.meta_description: Conversion behavior analytics that finds the moments where prospects commit or drift away across channels, and designs tested changes to improve conversion.
services.summary: Find the specific moments where prospects commit or drift away across digital, phone and in-person channels, and design tested changes that improve conversion.
services.lede: Conversion behavior analytics goes beyond funnel charts to identify the behavioral moments that decide whether a prospect becomes a customer. We trace the full journey across channels and pinpoint where commitment forms or quietly erodes.
challenge: Conventional funnel reports show where people leave, but rarely why. A drop between application start and submission might reflect a confusing form, an unexpected document request, a price surprise or a competitor's call. Many conversion journeys also span multiple channels and weeks: a prospect researches online, calls a branch, receives an email sequence and visits in person. When each touchpoint lives in a different system, the funnel becomes a series of disconnected snapshots that no single team owns.

As a result, conversion efforts often default to generic tactics: more traffic, more follow-up, more discounts. These can raise volume while hiding the real constraint. The organizations that improve conversion sustainably are those that understand the specific conversion points, the moments where a small change in behavior predicts a large change in outcome, and then design and test precisely for those moments rather than for the funnel as a whole. Conversion behavior analytics makes those moments visible.

approach.title: Walk the conversion journey
approach.body: We experience the journey as a prospect would, interview sales and service staff, and observe or record real sessions where possible. This identifies the decision points, anxieties and handoffs that shape conversion, and reveals where the documented process differs from what actually happens across web, phone, email and in-person channels.

approach.title: Locate the true conversion points
approach.body: We stitch together events across channels and model time-to-conversion with survival analysis and cohort comparisons. This shows which early behaviors, such as completing a specific step, returning within a window or engaging with a particular resource, most strongly predict conversion, and where different behavioral types stall for different reasons.

approach.title: Target the specific barrier
approach.body: For each priority conversion point we diagnose whether the barrier is motivation, ability or the absence of a timely prompt. We then design focused changes: simplified steps, clearer expectations, better-timed follow-up, reassurance at moments of risk, or revised sales handoffs. Each change is tied to a measurable hypothesis.

approach.title: Experiment at the decisive moments
approach.body: We design A/B tests or controlled pilots for each change, with power calculations sized to your traffic, a primary conversion metric and guardrails such as refund rates, complaint volume or downstream retention. This protects against improvements that raise conversion while harming customer quality or trust.

approach.title: Monitor conversion as a system
approach.body: Successful changes are rolled out with monitoring on the leading indicators that predict conversion. We build cross-channel conversion dashboards, align marketing, sales and service teams on shared definitions, and set up a backlog of next hypotheses so improvement continues after the engagement ends and new questions are tested in order of expected value.

deliverables: Cross-channel conversion journey map with handoffs
Conversion point analysis by behavioral type
Time-to-conversion survival curves and cohort views
Barrier diagnosis using motivation, ability and prompt
Experiment designs with power and guardrail metrics
Shared conversion dashboard and hypothesis backlog
outcomes: Teams know which specific moments matter most for conversion and why prospects stall there.
Marketing, sales and service share one view of the conversion journey across channels.
Conversion improvements are tested so they do not erode customer quality or trust.
Investment shifts from generic volume tactics to targeted, evidence-based changes.
services.who_we_serve: We support chief marketing and revenue officers, digital and ecommerce leaders, sales operations heads, admissions and enrollment directors, and membership executives. Typical clients include lenders, automotive retailers, health and fitness brands, software companies and associations. Engagements often begin when acquisition costs rise without matching growth, when a new channel is added, or when a redesigned site or application flow does not deliver the expected lift.
services.impact_lens: Conversion done well is about helping the right people complete decisions they already intend to make. Removing confusion from a mortgage application, an enrollment form or a health program signup reduces stress for customers and members. Staff spend less effort chasing poor-fit leads. We explicitly avoid dark patterns such as false urgency or hidden costs, because conversions gained through manipulation damage trust and tend to reverse.

faqs.q: What is a conversion point?
faqs.a: A conversion point is a specific behavioral moment that strongly predicts whether someone will ultimately convert, such as completing a key form section, returning within a certain window or speaking with a specialist. It is not necessarily the final purchase step. Finding conversion points lets teams focus on the moments with the greatest influence instead of spreading effort across the entire funnel.

faqs.q: Can you analyze conversion when part of the journey happens offline?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of the journeys we analyze include phone calls, branch or showroom visits, and paper or in-person steps. We link offline records such as call logs, appointment systems and CRM notes to digital events wherever identifiers allow, and use structured observation and interviews to fill gaps. Understanding the offline portion is often where the largest opportunities are found.

faqs.q: How do you avoid optimizing for short-term conversions at the expense of customer value?
faqs.a: Every experiment we design includes guardrail metrics that track downstream quality, such as early cancellation, returns, complaints, default risk or engagement after purchase. If a change lifts conversion but harms a guardrail, it is not recommended. We also evaluate conversion by behavioral type, since a change that helps one group can harm another.

faqs.q: How much traffic do we need for A/B testing conversion changes?
faqs.a: It depends on your baseline conversion rate and the smallest improvement worth detecting. We run power calculations before each test to determine required sample size and duration. When volume is low, we use sequential designs, larger and bolder changes, staged pilots or matched comparisons, and we are candid when a question cannot be answered reliably with the available volume.

services.name: Experimentation & A/B Testing
services.meta_description: A/B testing and experimentation consulting: hypothesis design, power analysis, guardrail metrics and pilots that give clear answers online and offline.
services.summary: Design experiments and pilots that produce clear, trustworthy answers, with proper power, guardrail metrics and behavioral hypotheses, in digital and offline settings.
services.lede: A/B testing is the most reliable way to learn what actually changes behavior. We design experiments and pilots with sound hypotheses, adequate power and guardrail metrics, whether you test web pages, sales scripts, care programs or policies.
challenge: Many organizations run tests that cannot answer their own questions. Sample sizes are too small to detect realistic effects. Tests are stopped the moment results look favorable, which inflates false positives. Several metrics are checked until one shows significance. Variants change many things at once, so even a clear winner explains little. Over time, leaders notice that winning tests do not add up to better performance, and confidence in experimentation erodes.

Outside digital products, experimentation is often considered impractical. Yet branch processes, outreach scripts, onboarding programs, clinical reminders and training initiatives can all be tested through randomized pilots, stepped rollouts or carefully matched comparisons. Organizations that only test button colors miss the larger opportunity: learning, with evidence, which operational and service changes actually shift customer, patient and employee behavior. A well-run experimentation program treats every significant change as a chance to learn, and builds a record of what works that compounds over time.

approach.title: Ground tests in real behavior
approach.body: We review your current testing practice, past results and decision process, and gather qualitative insight into the behavior each test is meant to change. Good experiments start from an understanding of why people act as they do, which leads to bolder, better-targeted variants than incremental guesswork.

approach.title: Choose metrics that matter
approach.body: We select a single primary metric linked to a predictive KPI, establish baselines and variance from historical data, and define guardrail metrics that would reveal harm, such as cancellations, complaints, error rates or downstream disengagement. Segment-level baselines help anticipate where effects may differ across behavioral types.

approach.title: Write the hypothesis and the plan
approach.body: Each experiment receives a written plan before launch: the behavioral hypothesis, the mechanism expected to drive change, randomization unit, minimum detectable effect, power calculation, test duration, stopping rules and analysis method. Internal pre-registration of this plan prevents after-the-fact metric shopping and makes results credible to skeptical stakeholders.

approach.title: Run and analyze with rigor
approach.body: We support implementation, monitor sample ratio and data quality during the test, and analyze results with appropriate methods, including confidence intervals, variance reduction where suitable and corrections for multiple comparisons. Results are reported in plain language with effect sizes and uncertainty, not just a pass or fail verdict.

approach.title: Build an experimentation capability
approach.body: We help establish a test backlog prioritized by expected value, templates for plans and readouts, a knowledge base of past results, and review practices that keep quality high. Training for product, marketing and operations teams turns experimentation from a specialist activity into a routine way of making decisions.

Accumulated test results become durable organizational knowledge rather than isolated wins.
services.who_we_serve: We work with product and growth leaders, marketing executives, heads of analytics and data science, operations leaders and program directors in health systems and associations. Clients range from software companies with mature A/B testing platforms that need sharper methodology, to lenders, retailers and nonprofits running their first randomized pilots. services.impact_lens: Rigorous experimentation protects people from well-intentioned changes that do not work or that cause unintended harm. Guardrail metrics surface effects on vulnerable groups before rollout. In health, education and community programs, testing ensures limited resources are spent on approaches that genuinely help. We follow ethical review practices appropriate to the setting, avoid deceptive variants, and ensure that experiments respect the autonomy and interests of participants.

faqs.q: What is a guardrail metric?
faqs.a: A guardrail metric is a measure you monitor during an experiment to make sure a change does not cause harm, even if it improves the primary metric. Examples include cancellation rates, complaint volume, page load time, error rates, refund requests or downstream retention. If a guardrail deteriorates beyond a predefined threshold, the variant is not shipped, regardless of how well it performs on the main goal.

faqs.q: Why does statistical power matter so much?
faqs.a: An underpowered test has a low chance of detecting a real effect, so it often reports no difference when one exists. Worse, when an underpowered test does show a significant result, the effect size is usually exaggerated. Calculating power before launch tells you how many participants and how much time you need, or whether a bolder change is required to make the test worthwhile.

faqs.q: Can we run experiments outside of digital products?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly design randomized pilots for outreach scripts, branch processes, appointment reminders, onboarding programs, training curricula and pricing communications. Randomization can occur at the level of customers, locations, teams or time periods. When full randomization is not feasible, stepped-wedge rollouts and matched comparison designs can still provide credible evidence.

faqs.q: Do we need a specific testing platform?
faqs.a: No. We work with whatever tools you already use, from commercial experimentation platforms to feature flag systems or manual assignment in a CRM. The methodology matters more than the platform. If your current tooling limits what you can learn, we will identify the gaps and recommend proportionate options rather than a wholesale replacement.

services.name: Behavioral Segmentation
services.meta_description: Behavioral segmentation that groups customers, members and patients by what they do, not demographics, so journeys and messages fit each type.
services.summary: Group customers, users, members and patients by how they actually behave, so every journey, message and service moment fits the people it is meant to reach.
services.lede: Behavioral segmentation groups people by what they do rather than who they are on paper. We build behavioral typologies from your data and research, so design, messaging and service decisions match how each type actually decides and acts.
challenge: Most segmentation schemes were built for media buying. They sort people by age, income, region or firmographic attributes, sometimes enriched with attitudes from a one-time survey. These segments look tidy in a presentation but struggle in practice: two people with identical demographics can behave in opposite ways, and the segments rarely tell a product or service team what to change. Over time the segmentation becomes a slide that teams politely ignore.

Meanwhile the behavioral differences that matter most go unnamed. Some customers research exhaustively and decide slowly. Some commit fast and then disengage. Some depend on a human advisor at a specific moment. Some patients adhere until a side effect, then quietly stop. These behavioral types cut across demographic lines, and each needs something different. Behavioral segmentation makes these patterns explicit, measurable and actionable, giving every team that touches the journey a shared map of who needs what, and when.

approach.title: Learn how people really decide
approach.body: Through interviews, contextual inquiry and review of service interactions, we collect rich descriptions of how different people approach the decision or behavior in question. This qualitative work, often supported by short diary studies, generates initial hypotheses about behavioral types and identifies the behavioral variables most likely to distinguish them.

approach.title: Build the behavioral typology
approach.body: We engineer behavioral features from event data, such as pace, sequence, channel preference, engagement depth and response to prompts, and apply clustering and latent class methods to identify stable groups. Each candidate segment is tested for distinctiveness, size, stability over time and its relationship to the outcomes that matter.

approach.title: Make each type actionable
approach.body: For each behavioral type we define how to identify it early, what it needs at each stage of the journey, and which barriers matter most using the motivation, ability and prompt lens. We translate these into journey variations, message strategies and service models, and create profiles that teams across the organization can use.

approach.title: Validate with targeted experiments
approach.body: We test whether tailored treatments outperform a single approach for each type, using A/B tests or pilots with segment-level analysis. We also validate classification rules on new cohorts to confirm that people can be assigned to a type accurately and early enough to make a difference.

approach.title: Operationalize the segments
approach.body: Segment assignment logic is implemented in your CRM, marketing platform or product so that teams can act on it in real time. We build segment-level dashboards, train staff to use the typology in daily work, and schedule periodic refreshes so the segmentation evolves as behavior changes.

Behavioral feature set and clustering analysis
Behavioral typology with profiles and sizing

Type-specific journey and messaging recommendations
Segment dashboards and refresh protocol

services.impact_lens: Segmenting by behavior respects people as individuals with different needs, rather than stereotypes defined by age or zip code. It allows organizations to give more support to those who are struggling and less friction to those who are ready. It also reduces the risk of demographic profiling. We design segments that are explainable, avoid proxies for protected characteristics, and serve the person's own goals.

faqs.q: How is behavioral segmentation different from personas?
faqs.a: Personas are often narrative composites based on limited interviews and are rarely tied to data. Behavioral segments are defined by measurable patterns of action, validated against outcomes and assignable to real individuals in your systems. We often create persona-style profiles to bring segments to life, but each one is grounded in observed behavior and can be tracked over time.

faqs.q: Do we need a lot of data to build behavioral segments?
faqs.a: More data helps, but it is not the only path. When behavioral history is limited, we combine smaller datasets with in-depth qualitative research and carefully designed surveys measuring behavioral tendencies. These can produce a provisional typology that is refined as more behavioral data accumulates. The important point is that segments describe behavior and are tested, not assumed.

faqs.q: Can behavioral segments change over time?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is a feature. People can move between types as their circumstances, experience and relationship with you change. We track transitions between segments, which often reveal valuable signals, such as an engaged customer shifting into a disengaging pattern. Refreshing the segmentation on a planned schedule keeps it aligned with current behavior.

faqs.q: How do you prevent segmentation from becoming discriminatory?
faqs.a: We review input variables for proxies of protected characteristics, test whether segment assignment produces disparate treatment across groups, and design interventions that add support rather than restrict access. Segments are documented so their logic can be explained to customers, regulators and staff. Fairness review is part of the method, not an afterthought.

services.name: Survey & Measurement Design
services.meta_description: Survey and measurement design grounded in psychometrics: reliable, valid instruments for customer, employee, patient and member insight that informs decisions.
services.summary: Build surveys and measurement instruments that are reliable, valid and ready to inform decisions, grounded in psychometrics rather than in guesswork.
services.lede: Good survey design is a measurement discipline. We apply psychometric methods to build customer, employee, patient and member instruments that are reliable, valid and short enough to complete, so the results support real decisions.
challenge: Surveys are among the most common tools organizations use to understand people, and among the most poorly built. Items are written by committee, double-barreled questions ask two things at once, scales shift between sections, and response options nudge people toward favorable answers. Instruments grow longer each year as new stakeholders add questions, and response rates fall. The resulting scores are tracked carefully, yet no one can say whether they measure what they claim.

The consequences are significant. Engagement scores that do not predict turnover, satisfaction scores that do not predict retention, and needs assessments that miss the most important needs all lead to misdirected investment. Psychometrics offers well-established tools for testing reliability and validity, but they are rarely applied outside academic research. Survey design grounded in measurement science changes what organizations can learn from the people they ask, and how much confidence they can place in the answers.

approach.title: Define the construct and the decision
approach.body: We begin by clarifying what you need to measure and what decision the measurement will inform. Through interviews and cognitive pretesting with members of the target population, we learn how people interpret the concepts in their own language. This ensures items reflect real experience rather than internal jargon.

approach.title: Assess existing instruments and data
approach.body: If you already run surveys, we analyze historical responses for internal consistency, factor structure, ceiling effects and item redundancy, and test whether scores relate to behavioral outcomes such as retention or adherence. This identifies items worth keeping, items to revise and gaps where key constructs are not measured at all.

approach.title: Build a sound instrument
approach.body: We write or adapt items using established principles: one idea per item, balanced response scales, neutral wording, logical flow and minimal burden. Where validated scales exist, we use them appropriately. We plan sampling, timing and mode to reduce nonresponse bias, and specify how scores will be calculated and interpreted.

approach.title: Pilot and validate
approach.body: The instrument is piloted with a representative sample. We evaluate reliability with internal consistency and test-retest methods, examine construct validity with factor analysis, and assess criterion validity by linking scores to subsequent behavior where possible. Underperforming items are revised or removed before full launch, and the final length is checked against completion data.

approach.title: Field, report and maintain
approach.body: We support fielding, design reports that show uncertainty and meaningful change rather than noise, and connect survey results to behavioral data for richer analysis. A measurement manual documents scoring and interpretation so the instrument remains consistent as staff change and can be revalidated periodically against new behavioral outcomes.

services.impact_lens: Every survey asks people for their time and candor. Well-designed instruments honor that by being shorter, clearer and more likely to lead to action. Employees and patients are more likely to be heard accurately when items are unbiased and accessible. Communities benefit when needs assessments capture real priorities. We design for readability, accessibility and cultural fit, and we protect respondent confidentiality throughout.

faqs.q: What do reliability and validity mean for a business survey?
faqs.a: Reliability means a survey produces consistent results: items intended to measure the same thing agree with each other, and scores are stable when nothing has changed. Validity means the survey measures what it is supposed to measure and relates to the outcomes it should predict. A reliable survey can still be invalid, so both must be tested before results are used for important decisions.

faqs.q: Can you improve our existing engagement or satisfaction survey?
faqs.a: Yes. We start with a psychometric audit of your historical data to see which items are performing, which are redundant and whether the overall scores relate to outcomes like turnover or retention. We then recommend targeted revisions that preserve trend comparability where it matters. Often a shorter, sharper version measures more effectively than the original.

faqs.q: Should we use a published validated scale or build our own?
faqs.a: When a well-validated scale fits your construct and population, using it saves time and allows benchmarking. Many organizational questions, however, are specific enough that custom items are needed. We often combine both, using established scales for core constructs and carefully developed items for context-specific topics, then validate the full instrument with your population.

faqs.q: How do you reduce survey fatigue and nonresponse?
faqs.a: We cut items that do not inform decisions, use adaptive logic so people only see relevant questions, design for mobile completion and explain how results will be used. Timing and invitation design also matter, and both can be tested. Closing the loop by showing respondents what changed based on their input is one of the strongest drivers of future participation.

services.name: Data Visualization & Decision Dashboards
services.meta_description: Data visualization and decision dashboard design that shows leaders predictive KPIs, uncertainty and the next action, built on how people read and decide.
services.summary: Design dashboards and visualizations around the decisions leaders actually make, showing predictive KPIs, uncertainty and the next action clearly.
services.lede: Decision dashboards should help people decide, not just display data. We design visualizations around specific decisions, predictive KPIs and the way people actually perceive information, so leaders see what matters and what to do next.
challenge: Many organizations have more dashboards than decisions. Each team builds its own views, metrics are defined slightly differently across them, and leaders flip between screens dense with charts, gauges and color. The visualization tools are powerful, but design choices often work against human perception: too many colors, truncated axes, cluttered layouts and no indication of whether a change is meaningful or noise. Usage typically peaks at launch and then declines.

The deeper problem is that most dashboards are designed around available data rather than around decisions. They answer what happened, but not whether it matters or what to do about it. When a dashboard does not connect to a decision and a predictive measure, people revert to spreadsheets and intuition. Good decision dashboards begin with the user, the decision and the behavior they are meant to support, and only then turn to the data required to inform it.

approach.title: Study how decisions are made
approach.body: We observe meetings, interview decision makers and watch how people currently use reports, spreadsheets and dashboards. Think-aloud sessions with existing tools reveal where people misread charts, lose context or abandon the screen. We document the recurring decisions, their timing and the questions that must be answered for each.

approach.title: Select the measures that matter
approach.body: Working from your KPI framework, we identify the predictive and lagging measures relevant to each decision, standardize definitions across teams, and determine how to represent uncertainty and normal variation. Where predictive KPIs do not yet exist, we flag the gap and link this work to KPI design.

approach.title: Design for perception and action
approach.body: We apply principles of visual perception, cognitive load and usability: appropriate chart types, consistent encodings, restrained color, clear hierarchy and annotations that explain change. Each view leads with the decision it supports, shows whether variation is meaningful, and points to the next action or drill-down.

approach.title: Usability test with real users
approach.body: Prototypes are tested with the people who will use them, using think-aloud protocols and task-based evaluation. We measure whether users can answer key questions accurately and quickly, identify misinterpretations, and iterate before engineering effort is committed. Accessibility checks ensure dashboards work for people with color vision differences and other needs.

approach.title: Build, adopt and govern
approach.body: We work with your BI or engineering team to implement the dashboards in your existing platform, then support adoption through training, meeting redesign and usage tracking. A governance model keeps metric definitions consistent and prevents the gradual clutter that undermines most dashboard programs over time.

faqs.q: Do you build dashboards or only design them?
faqs.a: We do both, depending on your needs. Many clients have capable BI teams and want design, user research and KPI expertise, so we deliver tested prototypes and specifications for their implementation. Others want end-to-end support, in which case we build within your existing platform. Either way, we design for maintainability by your team after the engagement.

faqs.q: Which BI tools do you work with?
faqs.a: We work within the platforms clients already own, including common commercial business intelligence tools and custom web visualizations. Good decision design principles apply across tools. If your platform imposes limits that undermine the decisions you need to support, we will describe the trade-offs and suggest pragmatic workarounds before recommending any change of platform.

faqs.q: How do you show uncertainty without confusing executives?
faqs.a: We use simple, tested conventions: shaded ranges for expected variation, clear markers when a change exceeds normal noise, and plain-language annotations. Usability testing confirms that leaders interpret these correctly. Showing uncertainty well actually reduces confusion, because it prevents overreaction to random fluctuations and focuses attention on changes that genuinely deserve a response.

faqs.q: Why do usability testing for an internal dashboard?
faqs.a: Internal users are still users, and their misreadings can cost far more than a confused website visitor. A misinterpreted chart can redirect a budget or a staffing plan. A few short think-aloud sessions typically reveal significant problems that designers and analysts could not see because they already know what the data means.

services.name: People Analytics
services.meta_description: People analytics consulting that links employee behavior, engagement and team dynamics to performance, with predictive measures and ethical data use.
services.summary: Connect employee behavior, engagement and team dynamics to performance with predictive measures, sound methods and an ethical approach to workforce data.
services.lede: People analytics should explain why teams perform, not just count headcount. We connect behavioral, survey and operational data to find the leading signals of engagement, retention and team effectiveness, and apply them ethically.
challenge: Human resources teams hold some of the richest behavioral data in any organization: hiring flows, internal mobility, learning activity, scheduling, collaboration patterns and engagement surveys. Yet much of it stays in separate systems, reported as descriptive counts such as headcount, turnover and training hours. Leaders learn that a valued team member is leaving when the resignation arrives, and they see engagement scores once a year, long after the conditions that shaped them have changed.

People analytics also carries real risks. Poorly designed models can embed bias, surveillance can damage trust, and correlations between activity metrics and performance are easy to misread. Organizations need an approach that is rigorous about measurement, transparent with employees and focused on improving the conditions for good work. Done well, people analytics helps leaders act earlier, and more fairly, on the conditions that drive retention, engagement and sustained team performance.

approach.title: Understand the work and the culture
approach.body: We interview leaders, managers and employees, observe how work flows across teams, and review existing HR, engagement and operational data. This grounds analysis in the realities of the organization and identifies the people outcomes that matter most, such as early tenure retention, manager effectiveness or team collaboration.

approach.title: Find the leading people signals
approach.body: We integrate HR, survey and operational data and use survival analysis, cohort comparisons and multilevel models to identify early signals of turnover, disengagement and performance. We distinguish individual, team and manager-level effects, because many apparent people problems are actually team, workload or system problems that no individual can solve alone.

approach.title: Design measures and interventions
approach.body: Signals are turned into predictive people KPIs and paired with interventions, such as onboarding redesign, manager coaching, workload adjustments or recognition practices. We apply self-determination theory and research on psychological safety to target autonomy, competence, belonging and trust, not just satisfaction, and we specify how each intervention is expected to change the leading signal it targets.

approach.title: Pilot and evaluate fairly
approach.body: Interventions are piloted with comparison groups where possible, and every model is audited for disparate impact across demographic groups. We evaluate both intended outcomes and unintended effects, such as increased workload or reduced trust, and refine designs with input from the employees involved before broader rollout.

approach.title: Build responsible capability
approach.body: We help HR and business leaders establish people analytics governance, including data use principles, employee communication and access controls. Dashboards are designed for managers, and leadership coaching helps them use the insights constructively. Your team gains methods, code and documentation to continue the work, along with a review cadence that keeps models current and fair.

faqs.q: How do you protect employee privacy in people analytics?
faqs.a: We follow data minimization, aggregate results to protect individuals, restrict access by role and avoid invasive monitoring of personal communications. We also recommend clear communication to employees about what data is used and why. Analyses that would identify individuals for adverse action are outside our scope. The goal is to improve the conditions of work, not to watch workers.

faqs.q: Can people analytics predict who will leave?
faqs.a: Analytics can identify patterns associated with higher turnover risk, such as particular onboarding experiences, workload patterns or team conditions. We focus on these conditions rather than labeling individuals, because acting on conditions is fairer and more effective. Predictions about individuals are probabilistic and should prompt supportive conversations, never punitive decisions.

faqs.q: How does people analytics connect to coaching and leadership development?
faqs.a: Analytics often reveals that outcomes vary more by team and manager than by individual. That points directly to leadership and team coaching as interventions. Our firm combines both capabilities, so insights from people analytics can inform coaching priorities, and coaching programs can be evaluated with the same measurement rigor applied to any other intervention.

faqs.q: What data sources are typically involved?
faqs.a: Common sources include HR information systems, applicant tracking, learning platforms, engagement and pulse surveys, performance processes, scheduling and operational data. We start with what is readily available and valuable, and only add sources when they answer a clear question. More data is not always better, especially when it raises privacy concerns.

services.name: Behavioral Design Consulting
services.meta_description: Behavioral design consulting that diagnoses why people do not act and designs tested, ethical changes to products, services and messages that make action easy.
services.summary: Diagnose why people are not acting and design focused, ethical changes to products, services and communications that make the desired behavior easier.
services.lede: Behavioral design consulting applies behavioral science to the practical question of why people do not act, and what would help them. We diagnose the real barrier, design a targeted change and test it before it scales.
challenge: Organizations invest heavily in persuading people to act: to buy, enroll, renew, adhere, complete training or adopt a new tool. When the behavior does not follow, the usual response is more communication, more incentives or more features. These efforts often fail because they address the wrong barrier. A customer who is already motivated but finds the process confusing does not need another persuasive email. A patient who understands the benefit but forgets at the critical moment needs a prompt, not an education campaign.

Behavioral science offers a sharper diagnosis. The Fogg Behavior Model holds that behavior happens when motivation, ability and a prompt converge at the same moment. Behavioral economics explains why defaults, framing, friction and timing carry so much weight. Yet these ideas are frequently applied as a loose collection of nudges rather than as a disciplined design process. Effective behavioral design consulting starts with a precise target behavior, diagnoses the specific gap, and treats every intervention as a hypothesis to be tested.

approach.title: Define the target behavior in context
approach.body: We translate a broad goal, such as better retention or higher adoption, into specific behaviors performed by specific people at specific moments. Interviews, contextual inquiry and journey mapping reveal what those people are trying to accomplish, what competes for their attention, and where the current experience makes the desired action harder than it needs to be.

approach.title: Locate where behavior breaks down
approach.body: Behavioral data shows where people stall, delay or abandon, and which behavioral types struggle most. We combine these signals with the qualitative findings to diagnose, at each critical moment, whether the shortfall is in motivation, in ability (time, effort, cognitive load, cost, routine), or in the presence and timing of a prompt.

approach.title: Design the smallest effective change
approach.body: We design interventions matched to the diagnosed barrier: simplifying steps, changing defaults, reframing choices, adding timely prompts, building commitment devices, or redesigning a service handoff. Each intervention is specified with the behavior it targets, the mechanism expected to work, and the predictive KPI it should move. Ethical review is built into the design brief.

approach.title: Prototype, pilot and measure
approach.body: Interventions are prototyped and tested with real users before launch, then evaluated through A/B tests or controlled pilots with guardrail metrics. We report effects by behavioral type, because a change that helps one group can leave another behind. Interventions that do not work are documented as learning, not buried as failures.

approach.title: Embed behavior change in operations
approach.body: Successful interventions are built into products, processes, scripts and training, with ownership assigned and leading indicators monitored. We help teams adopt a behavioral design playbook and coach leaders to apply the motivation, ability and prompt lens in their own decisions, so the organization keeps improving without outside help.

services.who_we_serve: Our behavioral design consulting serves chief executives, chief marketing and experience officers, product leaders, health system and health plan executives, association leaders and public program directors. Organizations call us when a launch underperforms, when engagement or adherence has plateaued, when a costly program is not changing behavior, or when leadership wants a disciplined, evidence-based alternative to generic nudge tactics. We also advise founders building behavior change into a product from the start.
services.impact_lens: Behavioral design is most valuable when it helps people achieve their own goals: taking medication as prescribed, saving for the future, completing an education, using a tool that makes work easier. Customers face less friction, employees spend less effort working around poor processes, and communities benefit from programs that actually change behavior. We hold a firm line against manipulation, designing only interventions that people would endorse if they understood how they work.

faqs.q: What is behavioral design?
faqs.a: Behavioral design is the practice of applying behavioral science to the design of products, services, processes and communications so that desired behaviors become easier and more likely. It draws on psychology, behavioral economics and human-computer interaction. Unlike traditional design, it starts from a specific target behavior and a diagnosis of why that behavior is not occurring, then tests whether the design actually changes it.

faqs.q: How is behavioral design different from nudging?
faqs.a: Nudges, such as defaults, reminders and social norms, are one category of tool within behavioral design. Behavioral design is broader: it includes diagnosing the barrier, redesigning entire journeys and services, building skills and confidence, and changing the environment around a behavior. Nudges work best when they address the correct barrier, which is why diagnosis comes first in our process.

faqs.q: What does the Fogg Behavior Model add to the process?
faqs.a: The model gives teams a simple and practical diagnostic: behavior happens when motivation, ability and a prompt converge. When a behavior is not happening, it helps identify which element is missing. That prevents common misfires, such as adding incentives when the real issue is complexity. We use it alongside other frameworks, including self-determination theory and health behavior models, depending on the context.

faqs.q: How do you make sure behavioral design is ethical?
faqs.a: Every intervention passes an ethical review that asks whether it serves the person's own interests, whether it is transparent, whether people can easily opt out, and whether it would be acceptable if made public. We decline work that relies on deception, exploits vulnerabilities or creates hidden costs. Ethical design also performs better over time because it builds trust instead of eroding it.

services.name: Customer Journey Mapping
services.meta_description: Customer journey mapping that combines research and behavioral data to show where people commit, stall or leave, and which moments deserve redesign and testing.
services.summary: Map the real journey your customers, members or patients take, combining research with behavioral data to find the moments that decide outcomes.
services.lede: Customer journey mapping is only useful when it reflects what people actually experience. We combine field research with behavioral data from your systems to build journey maps that pinpoint the moments where people commit, stall or leave.
challenge: Many journey maps are built in a workshop from internal assumptions. Teams place sticky notes along an idealized path, add emotion curves based on intuition, and produce an attractive poster. The resulting map often mirrors the organization chart more than the customer's experience. It omits the phone call made out of confusion, the competitor website visited between steps, the family member consulted before a decision, and the long silence before cancellation.

Because they are not grounded in evidence, such maps rarely change decisions. They also tend to treat every step as equally important, which spreads improvement effort thinly. Effective customer journey mapping identifies which moments carry disproportionate weight, links each stage to measurable behavior, and shows how different behavioral types travel different paths. That turns the map from a communication artifact into a working tool for prioritization, design and ongoing measurement.

approach.title: Research the lived journey
approach.body: We conduct interviews, contextual inquiry, diary studies and service safaris with customers and frontline staff, capturing what people do, think and feel at each step, including the steps that happen outside your channels. We pay particular attention to workarounds, moments of uncertainty and the points where people seek help from someone else.

approach.title: Overlay behavioral data
approach.body: We link each journey stage to events in your systems, measure time between stages, and calculate where people drop out or loop back. Cohort and survival analysis show which stages most strongly predict the eventual outcome. This reveals conversion points and highlights the gap between the journey people describe and the one the data records.

approach.title: Build an evidence-based journey map
approach.body: We create journey maps that show stages, actions, thoughts, emotions, channels, supporting processes and data signals together, with variations for key behavioral types. Each moment of truth is annotated with its evidence, its diagnosed barrier and opportunity hypotheses. A service blueprint layer connects frontstage experience to backstage processes.

approach.title: Validate and prioritize opportunities
approach.body: We validate the map with customers and staff, then prioritize opportunities by expected impact, effort and confidence. The highest priority ideas are prototyped and tested through usability sessions, pilots or A/B tests, so the map leads directly to measured improvement rather than a long, unfunded wish list.

approach.title: Keep the map alive
approach.body: We connect the journey map to dashboards tracking the key stage metrics, assign owners to critical moments across departments, and set a cadence for updating the map as products, policies and behavior change. Teams learn to use the map in planning, design reviews and cross-functional problem solving.

Evidence-based journey maps by behavioral type
Stage-level metrics linked to source system events
Moments of truth with diagnosed barriers and hypotheses
Service blueprint connecting frontstage and backstage
Prioritized opportunity roadmap with test plans

Improvement effort concentrates on the moments that most influence outcomes.
